question:
(i) Explain how the line spectrum of hydrogen is produced due to transitions between energy levels.
(ii) Why are energy changes in nuclear processes generally much larger than those in atomic spectral transitions? Use the mass-energy relation in your answer.

options.A:
(i) Hydrogen gives a continuous spectrum because electrons can change energy by arbitrary amounts.
(ii) Nuclear energies are smaller because mass defect is not associated with energy.
options.B:
(i) Line spectra arise from nuclear transitions of protons in hydrogen.
(ii) Atomic and nuclear energy changes are always equal.
options.C:
(i) Hydrogen lines result from photons of the same energy in all transitions.
(ii) Nuclear processes are weaker because $c^2$ is small.
options.D:
(i) Hydrogen electrons occupy discrete levels; a transition from $E_i$ to $E_f$ emits a photon with $h\nu=E_i-E_f$. Only definite energy differences occur, so the spectrum has lines.
(ii) Nuclear processes involve mass defect, and $E=\Delta mc^2$. Since $c^2$ is very large, even a small mass change produces much larger energy than atomic electronic transitions.
